young.html: Thorstein Veblen (say VEB-len) grew up on a farm in Wisconsin and Minnesota, the son of Norwegian settlers. When he became a professor, he looked at rich people's habits like a scientist watching a strange tribe.

He noticed something odd. Some people buy things not because they work better, but because they are expensive, so others can see how much money they have. A silver spoon made by hand stirs soup no better than a plain spoon from a machine, but it costs much more, and that, Veblen said, is part of why people want it. He called this conspicuous consumption: spending in a way that shows off.

young.name: gb-veblen-spoons
young.cap: Two spoons that do the same job. Tap through what each one "says."

young.html: Spot the show-off. Look through a catalog or a store together. Find something that costs much more than a plain version that does the same job. Why might someone buy it? Is it always showing off, or can it be quality, beauty or a gift? Veblen's critics said he forgot those reasons.

full.html: Thorstein Veblen (1857–1929) was an economist and social critic who taught at Chicago, Stanford and other universities. The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), his first book, was a sharp, ironic look at the wealthy families of America's Gilded Age, written in the cool language of a scientist describing customs. Its phrases have entered everyday speech.

Veblen traces the "leisure class" back to early societies where the strong took the honored work of war and hunting and left the daily drudgery to others. Ever since, he argues, avoiding useful work and spending lavishly have been marks of status. The key is that wealth must be seen:

full.text: In order to gain and to hold the esteem of men it is not sufficient merely to possess wealth or power. The wealth or power must be put in evidence, for esteem is awarded only on evidence.
full.author: Thorstein Veblen
full.work: The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter III (Conspicuous Leisure)
full.ed: The Macmillan Company, New York (copyright 1899; 1908 printing)

Showing status by spending on costly goods others can see.

full.html: In his chapter on taste, Veblen argues that our very sense of beauty gets mixed up with cost. His example is a hand-wrought silver spoon, worth some ten to twenty dollars, which is no more useful than a machine-made one, and perhaps no more useful than an aluminum spoon costing a few cents. Much of the handmade spoon's beauty, he says, is really its expense.

full.name: gb-veblen-demand
full.cap: Slide the price. For most goods, people buy less as the price rises. For a status good, a higher price can make it more wanted, at least for a while. (An illustration, not real data.)

full.title: Reading a demand table
full.q: A shop finds that at \$50 it sells 20 handbags a week, and at \$80 it sells 26. By what percent did the quantity sold change, and does this look like an ordinary good or the "Veblen effect"?
steps: The price went up and sales went up too, the reverse of the usual law of demand.
full.a: Up 30%; it looks like the Veblen effect (though other causes, such as a change in fashion, would need ruling out).

full.html: The book made Veblen famous and gave economics and sociology lasting terms. Economists later named goods whose demand rises with price "Veblen goods," though they are rare and hard to prove in data. Studies of status, signaling and consumer behavior have built on his ideas. Critics have pointed out that Veblen relied on examples and irony rather than systematic evidence; that people buy costly things for many reasons, including quality, craftsmanship, durability and the pleasure of beauty; and that his own tone was often contemptuous of the people he studied. Defenders reply that his central point, that much spending is about how we look to others, is now widely accepted.
Thinking Veblen said everyone who buys a nice thing is showing off. He described a tendency in how status works, mainly among the very wealthy of his time.

items: Adam Smith, whose Wealth of Nations is in the 18th-century rungs, wrote in his earlier Theory of Moral Sentiments that people seek wealth partly to be noticed and admired; Veblen made that the center of his theory.
Rousseau's Discourses blamed society's ills on comparison and the wish to be esteemed; compare Veblen's "invidious comparison."
Tawney's Acquisitive Society, the next rung, also criticizes wealth that is cut off from useful work.
Fitzgerald's Great Gatsby, in the literature rungs, shows lavish parties and display in the 1920s.
The Economics Ladder topic on the law of demand explains the ordinary pattern that Veblen goods seem to break.
